analogy.p: Picture walkers who must cross a high mountain pass to reach the next valley. The pass is the activation energy: very few walkers have enough energy to climb it, so only a few cross each hour. Now a tunnel is dug through the mountain (the catalyst), giving a lower, easier route. More walkers make the journey every hour, so the rate goes up, yet every walker still starts in the same valley and ends in the same valley (same reactants and products, same overall energy change) and the tunnel is still there afterwards. The analogy breaks down because a real catalyst actually takes part in the reaction (reactants bond to its surface temporarily), whereas a tunnel is only a passive route.

bullets: A catalyst **increases the rate of reaction**: more product forms in each second.
It is **not used up** in the reaction, so its mass at the end equals its mass at the start (though a solid catalyst can change physically, for example lumps breaking into powder).
It does **not appear in the balanced equation** because it is neither a reactant nor a product. It is usually written **above the reaction arrow**, for example MnO₂ above 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂.
Only a **small amount** is needed because the catalyst keeps being regenerated.
**Different reactions need different catalysts**: a catalyst that works for one reaction may do nothing for another.
**Enzymes** are the catalysts of living things (biological catalysts).
Mark-scheme wording to learn: 'a catalyst **speeds up** a reaction by providing an **alternative pathway** with a **lower activation energy**, and is **not used up**'.
core.p: A **catalyst** is a substance that **speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up** in the reaction. It takes part in the reaction mechanism but is regenerated at the end, so the same catalyst can be used again and again and only a small amount is needed to speed up a very large amount of reactant. Catalysts are central to chemistry because they let industry and living things make useful products quickly, at lower temperatures and with less energy. AQA expects you to state this definition exactly, to know that different reactions need different catalysts, and to explain how a catalyst works in terms of **activation energy**.

bullets: Particles in a gas or solution are constantly moving and colliding, but **most collisions do not lead to reaction** because the particles do not have enough energy.
A collision that has at least the activation energy is called a **successful collision** (an effective collision).
Rate depends on **how often** collisions happen and **what fraction** of them have enough energy.
Raising **temperature** gives particles more energy and makes them move faster: collisions are more frequent **and** more of them are successful.
Raising **concentration** or **pressure** (gases) packs more particles into the same volume so collisions are more frequent.
Increasing **surface area** of a solid exposes more particles to collisions.

A **catalyst** works differently from all of these: it lowers the activation energy so that a larger **proportion** of collisions is successful, without needing any change in temperature or concentration.
core.h: Reminder: rate of reaction and collision theory
core.p: To understand catalysts you must be secure on collision theory. Chemical reactions can only happen when reactant particles **collide**, and the collision must have **enough energy** to break the bonds in the reactants. The minimum energy that colliding particles must have in order to react is the **activation energy**. The **rate of reaction** depends on the **frequency of successful collisions**, meaning the number of collisions per second that have at least the activation energy. Anything that increases the frequency of successful collisions increases the rate.

bullets: Activation energy is shown on a reaction profile as the **height of the energy hill** from the energy of the reactants up to the peak of the curve.
Its units are usually **kJ/mol** (or kJ), and it is always a **positive** value.
Activation energy is **not the same as the overall energy change (ΔH)**: ΔH is the difference between reactants and products, while activation energy is the barrier between them.
Reactions with high activation energies (for example the reaction of nitrogen with hydrogen) are very slow without a catalyst or very high temperatures.
Heating increases the number of particles with enough energy but **does not change the activation energy itself**.
A catalyst is one of the very few things that **does change the activation energy** of the route taken by the reaction.
core.p: **Activation energy** is the minimum amount of energy that particles must have when they collide for the reaction to happen. Think of it as the energy needed to start breaking the old bonds so that new bonds can form. Every reaction has an activation energy, even highly exothermic ones such as burning, which is why a fuel needs a spark or flame to start burning. A **high activation energy** means few collisions are successful and the reaction is slow at that temperature, whereas a **low activation energy** means many collisions are successful and the reaction is fast.

bullets: Say it as a chain of reasoning: catalyst → **alternative pathway** → **lower activation energy** → **more particles have enough energy** → **more frequent successful collisions** → **faster rate**.
The catalyst does **not** increase the energy of the particles and does **not** make particles move faster.
The catalyst does **not** increase the number of collisions overall; it increases the **proportion that are successful**.
Solid catalysts are often used as **powders, pellets or fine meshes** because a bigger **surface area** gives more places for reactions to happen.
The reaction at the surface goes through stages: **adsorption** of reactants, reaction (bonds weaken and new bonds form), then **desorption** of products.
Because the catalyst surface is not used up, it can be **reused**, although it can slowly become coated or poisoned.
core.h: How a catalyst works: an alternative pathway
core.p: A catalyst provides a **different reaction pathway** (an alternative route) from reactants to products, and this new pathway has a **lower activation energy**. Because the energy barrier is lower, a bigger proportion of the colliding particles have at least the activation energy at the same temperature, so the **frequency of successful collisions increases** and the rate goes up. With many solid catalysts the reactant particles stick (adsorb) onto the surface of the catalyst, which weakens their bonds and holds them close together so they react more easily, and then the product particles leave the surface so it is free for the next reactants.

bullets: **Same start and same finish**: the reactants and products are the same chemicals, so their energies cannot change.
**Lower peak** for the catalysed curve: this shows the lower activation energy (Ea).
**ΔH is unchanged**: for an exothermic reaction the products are lower than the reactants by the same amount whether or not a catalyst is used.
Label the vertical axis **Energy** and the horizontal axis **Progress of reaction** (or 'Reaction coordinate').
Draw the activation energy as a **vertical arrow from the reactant level up to the peak**, and the overall energy change as a **vertical arrow between reactant and product levels**.
The same ideas apply to an **endothermic** reaction: the products are higher than the reactants, and a catalyst still just lowers the peak.
Exam trap: do **not** draw the catalysed curve ending at a different product level.
core.h: Reaction profiles with and without a catalyst
core.p: A **reaction profile** plots the energy of the chemicals against the progress of the reaction. The curve starts at the energy of the reactants, rises to a peak (the top of the activation energy hill) and then falls to the energy of the products. For a catalysed reaction you draw a **second curve with a lower peak**, but starting at the same reactant level and ending at the same product level. This shows visually that the catalyst lowers the activation energy but does not change the overall energy change.

bullets: It does **not** change the **products** formed.
It does **not** change the **amount (yield)** of product in a reaction that goes to completion: the same total volume of gas is collected in the end.
It does **not** change the **overall energy change** (ΔH) of the reaction.
It does **not** increase the energy of the reacting particles.
It is **not used up**, so it is not counted as a reactant in calculations.
It does **not** work on every reaction: catalysts are **specific**.
It does **not** make a reversible reaction favour the products; it speeds up forward and reverse reactions **equally**.
core.h: What a catalyst does NOT do
core.p: Many marks are lost by students who credit catalysts with abilities they do not have. A catalyst changes **how fast** a reaction goes, not **what** happens. It does not make a reaction that is impossible possible, it does not produce more product from the same amount of reactant, and it does not change the energy released or absorbed. It also is not a reactant, so it is not included in the balanced equation and it is not listed when you calculate reacting masses or moles.

bullets: Forward and reverse reactions are both sped up **equally**.
The **equilibrium composition** (the amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium) is **unchanged**.
The catalyst helps **time**, not **yield**.

In the Haber process the temperature is a **compromise**: a higher temperature speeds the reaction but lowers the equilibrium yield of ammonia; the **iron catalyst** lets a moderate temperature (about 450 °C) give an acceptable rate.
For **Higher tier** Le Chatelier's principle: changing temperature, pressure or concentration shifts equilibrium, but a **catalyst does not shift it**.
Exam phrase: 'a catalyst increases the rate at which equilibrium is reached but does not change the position of equilibrium'.
core.p: In a reversible reaction a catalyst speeds up **both** the forward and the reverse reactions by the same factor, because it lowers the activation energy of the pathway in both directions. This means the **position of equilibrium does not change**, and the equilibrium yield is the same with or without a catalyst. What the catalyst does is let the reaction **reach equilibrium sooner**. This is why the Haber process uses an iron catalyst: it does not give more ammonia at equilibrium, but it gives the ammonia much faster at a temperature that would otherwise be far too slow.

bullets: Enzymes are **biological catalysts**: they speed up reactions in cells without being used up.
Each enzyme is **specific** to one substrate because the shape of its active site only fits that substrate.
A high temperature or the wrong pH **denatures** the enzyme: the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits.
Typical human enzymes work best at about **37 °C**; industrial enzymes may be chosen to tolerate other conditions.
Enzymes work in **mild conditions** (body temperature, neutral pH), which is why they are valuable in industry for saving energy.
Example: **catalase** breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂.
Link: this topic connects chemistry's **catalysts** to biology's **enzymes**, so be ready to write about either.
core.p: **Enzymes** are the catalysts of living organisms. Enzymes are **proteins** made of long chains of amino acids folded into a specific three-dimensional shape that includes an **active site**. The substrate fits into the active site (the 'lock and key' idea), the reaction takes place, and the products leave, leaving the enzyme unchanged. Enzymes are essential for digestion, respiration and photosynthesis and for industrial processes such as making yoghurt, cheese, fruit juice and biological washing powders. Because they are proteins, enzymes work best at an **optimum temperature and pH** and are **denatured** when conditions are too extreme.

bullets: **Iron** in the Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.
**Nickel** in the hydrogenation of alkenes to alkanes, as used to harden vegetable oils into margarine.
**Manganese(IV) oxide (MnO₂)** or the enzyme **catalase** in the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.
**Aluminium oxide** (or zeolite) in the **catalytic cracking** of long-chain alkanes into shorter alkanes and alkenes.
**Platinum, palladium and rhodium** in a car's **catalytic converter**, speeding up the conversion of carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides into carbon dioxide and nitrogen.
**Transition metals and their compounds** are often good catalysts (a property you learn in the periodic table topic).
Do not state a catalyst 'for all reactions': always name the **reaction** it is used in.
core.h: Examples of catalysts you should know
core.p: Specific catalysts for specific reactions appear regularly in exam questions, particularly in industrial processes. You should link each catalyst to its reaction, and be able to say that it speeds up the process without being used up. Catalysts are often **transition metals or their compounds**, which is a link to the properties of transition metals in the periodic table topic. Remember that the exact catalyst belongs to the exact reaction, so do not swap them around.

bullets: **Advantages**: faster reaction, **lower energy use**, lower operating temperatures, **less fossil fuel burned**, more product in less time.
Lower temperatures can also mean **fewer unwanted side reactions** and safer operation.
Catalysts are **not used up**, so they are **reused**, but they must be **separated** from the products (easier for solid catalysts with liquid or gas reactants).
**Disadvantages**: some catalysts are **expensive** (platinum, palladium, rhodium), some are **toxic** or hazardous, and catalysts may be **poisoned** by impurities in the reactants.
A catalyst only changes **rate**: the plant still needs raw materials, so a catalyst is not a free supply of product.
In a data question, weigh up **cost of catalyst** against **savings in energy and time**.
Sustainability link: reduced energy demand means a **smaller carbon footprint** for the process.
core.h: Why industry uses catalysts: costs, energy and the environment
core.p: Catalysts make industrial processes **cheaper and more sustainable**. Because a catalyst lowers the activation energy, the reaction can run quickly at a **lower temperature and pressure**, which saves energy (fuel), reduces the cost of building strong equipment and reduces the carbon dioxide released by burning fuels to heat the reactors. Faster reactions also mean more product per hour. On the downside, catalysts, especially those made of **precious metals** such as platinum, can be expensive, and they can be **poisoned** (coated by impurities so that the surface no longer works) so reactants must be purified and catalysts sometimes replaced.

bullets: **Independent variable**: the catalyst (or its presence); **dependent variable**: volume of oxygen collected over time.
**Control variables**: volume and concentration of hydrogen peroxide, **mass** of catalyst, particle size/surface area of catalyst, temperature, and the apparatus used.

Method: measure a fixed volume of hydrogen peroxide into a conical flask, add the catalyst quickly, **immediately bung the flask** connected to the gas syringe and **start the stopwatch**, then record the volume every 10 or 15 seconds.
Repeat with each catalyst, and repeat each one to find a **mean** and spot anomalies.
Plot **volume against time** and compare **gradients** (steeper = faster).
**Safety**: wear **eye protection**; hydrogen peroxide can irritate skin and eyes; do not let the syringe plunger fly out; wash splashes with plenty of water.
To show the catalyst is not used up, **filter, dry and reweigh** it at the end: the mass is unchanged.
core.h: Investigating the effect of a catalyst
core.p: A common investigation uses **hydrogen peroxide** solution, which decomposes slowly to water and oxygen, and adds different solid catalysts such as manganese(IV) oxide, copper(II) oxide or pieces of liver or potato (which contain catalase). The rate is found by **measuring the volume of oxygen collected** in a gas syringe (or by displacement of water in an upturned measuring cylinder) at regular time intervals. A valid comparison needs a **fair test**: only the type of catalyst should change, while every other variable stays the same.

bullets: Mean rate = **quantity of reactant used** ÷ **time taken**, or mean rate = **quantity of product formed** ÷ **time taken**.
Units depend on the quantity: **g/s**, **cm³/s** or **mol/s**.
At any one moment the rate is the **gradient of the line**; for **Higher tier**, draw a **tangent** to the curve at that time and calculate rise ÷ run.
The gradient is **steepest at the start** because the concentration of reactants is highest, then decreases to zero when the reaction is complete.
A **flat (horizontal) line** means the reaction has finished.
Compare catalysed and uncatalysed curves: the catalysed one has a **steeper start** and **reaches the plateau sooner**, but both plateaus are at the **same volume**.
If two curves finish at **different heights**, a different amount of reactant was used, not a different catalyst.
core.p: The progress of a reaction is often shown by a graph of the quantity of product formed (such as gas volume) against time. The **steeper the line, the faster the rate**. When the line becomes horizontal the reaction has stopped because one reactant has been used up, so with the same amounts of reactants a catalysed and uncatalysed reaction **finish at the same height**, but the catalysed curve rises faster and levels off sooner. The **mean rate** is the amount of product formed (or reactant used up) divided by the time taken.

bullets: **Temperature up**: particles move faster and have more energy, so collisions are **more frequent** and a **greater proportion** have energy above the activation energy.
**Concentration / pressure up**: more particles in the same volume, so collisions are **more frequent** (the particles are closer together).
**Surface area up**: more particles of the solid are exposed to collisions, so collisions are more frequent.
**Catalyst added**: an **alternative pathway with lower activation energy**, so a **greater proportion** of collisions are successful.
Only **temperature** changes the average energy of the particles; only a **catalyst** changes the activation energy.
None of these changes the **amount of product** formed in the end (unless you change the amount of reactant).
core.h: Catalysts compared with other ways of speeding up a reaction
core.p: There are five factors in AQA's rate topic: temperature, concentration (or pressure for gases), surface area of solids, and catalysts. It is worth being able to compare them. All of them increase the **frequency of successful collisions**, but they do so in different ways, and the exam often asks you to choose the right explanation. A catalyst is the only one of these factors that works by **lowering the activation energy**.

bullets: **Energy changes**: reaction profiles; bond breaking needs energy, which is the idea behind activation energy.
**Organic chemistry**: catalytic cracking uses a hot catalyst to break long alkanes into smaller, more useful molecules.
**Haber process**: iron catalyst; the compromise of temperature, pressure and catalyst to balance rate and yield (Higher tier uses Le Chatelier).
**Atmosphere**: the catalytic converter lowers emissions of CO, NOx and unburnt hydrocarbons.
**Biology**: enzymes, denaturation, optimum temperature and pH, digestion enzymes (amylase, protease, lipase).
**Periodic table**: transition metals and their compounds are useful catalysts.
**Sustainability**: catalysts reduce energy costs and carbon footprint in industry.
core.p: Catalysts appear throughout GCSE science, so recognising the links helps you answer synoptic questions that combine ideas from several topics. In chemistry they link to energy changes (reaction profiles and activation energy), to organic chemistry (cracking, hydrogenation), to the Haber process and equilibria, to the atmosphere (catalytic converters), and to the periodic table (transition metals). In biology they link directly to enzymes in digestion and metabolism.

exam: **1 mark** 'State what a catalyst does': 'speeds up a reaction without being used up'. Write both parts.
**2 marks** 'Explain how a catalyst speeds up a reaction': 'provides an alternative pathway (1) with a lower activation energy (1)'.
**3 to 4 marks** 'Explain': link the chain: lower activation energy → more particles have enough energy → more frequent successful collisions → faster rate.
For **reaction profile** questions: both curves start and finish at the same levels; the catalysed curve has a **lower peak**; label **Ea** with an arrow and **ΔH** with an arrow.
Command words: **State** = brief fact; **Describe** = say what happens; **Explain** = give reasons using 'because' or 'so'; **Suggest** = apply knowledge to an unfamiliar situation.
**Graph questions**: compare gradients (steeper = faster), say both levels off at the **same volume**, and use data from the graph with units (for example 'it took 30 s compared with 240 s').
**Rate calculation**: mean rate = quantity ÷ time; show working and give the **unit** (cm³/s, g/s). Higher tier: tangent to the curve, rise ÷ run.

**Required practical wording**: name the independent, dependent and control variables, and say how you would make the test fair (same mass of catalyst, same concentration and volume of hydrogen peroxide, same temperature).
**Evaluation** (6 marks): give advantages (faster, cheaper energy, less CO₂) and disadvantages (cost of catalyst, poisoning, separation), then a **justified conclusion**.
Never write that a catalyst 'increases the energy' or 'is used up'; these lose the mark immediately.
Use the **exact board terminology**: 'alternative pathway', 'activation energy', 'not used up', 'frequency of successful collisions'.

mistakes.r: A catalyst is NOT used up; it is unchanged at the end and can be reused.
mistakes.w: A catalyst is used up in the reaction.

mistakes.r: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a LOWER ACTIVATION ENERGY; it does not increase the energy of the particles.
mistakes.w: A catalyst gives the particles more energy.

mistakes.r: It increases the PROPORTION (frequency) of SUCCESSFUL collisions because more particles have at least the activation energy.
mistakes.w: A catalyst increases the number of collisions.

mistakes.r: A catalyst does not change the amount of product or the position of equilibrium; it only changes how fast the reaction happens.
mistakes.w: A catalyst increases the yield / makes more product.

mistakes.r: Catalysts are not written in the balanced equation; they are written above the arrow.
mistakes.w: Catalysts are reactants so they go into the balanced equation.

mistakes.r: Reactants and products stay at the same energy; only the peak (activation energy) is lower.
mistakes.w: A catalysed reaction profile ends at a lower energy level.

mistakes.r: A catalyst does not change the temperature; it allows the reaction to work well at a lower temperature.
mistakes.w: A catalyst lowers the temperature of the reaction.

mistakes.r: Different reactions need different catalysts; each catalyst is specific.
mistakes.w: One catalyst works for all reactions.

mistakes.r: It makes the activation energy LOWER, not zero.
mistakes.w: The catalyst makes the activation energy zero.

summary: You must know that a catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up by giving it an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, how this changes reaction profiles and rate graphs, and that different reactions need different catalysts (enzymes in living things). It matters because catalysts make industrial processes faster, cheaper and less energy hungry, and it is a regular exam topic for describing, explaining and graph questions.

terms.d: A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up in the reaction.
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have in order to react when they collide.
A different reaction route with a lower activation energy that a catalyst provides.
How fast reactants are used up or products are formed; the amount of reactant used or product formed per unit time.
Chemical reactions can only occur when reacting particles collide with sufficient energy.
A collision between particles that has at least the activation energy, so a reaction occurs.
The number of collisions between particles in a given time.
A diagram showing the relative energies of reactants and products and the activation energy of a reaction.
A biological catalyst, a protein that speeds up reactions in living things.
The part of an enzyme with a specific shape where the substrate binds.
When an enzyme's shape (including the active site) is changed by high temperature or wrong pH so that it no longer works.
The quantity of reactant used or product formed divided by the time taken.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
When impurities bind to the surface of a catalyst so it can no longer speed up the reaction.
A reaction where the products can react to form the original reactants.

worked.ans: Without catalyst 0.25 cm³/s; with catalyst 2.0 cm³/s; the catalysed reaction is 8 times faster (the total volume, 60 cm³, is the same because a catalyst does not change the yield).
worked.q: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes to water and oxygen. Without a catalyst, 60 cm³ of oxygen is collected in 240 s. With manganese(IV) oxide, the same 60 cm³ is collected in 30 s. Calculate the mean rate in each case and state how many times faster the catalysed reaction is. (4 marks)
steps: Mean rate = volume of gas ÷ time taken.

worked.ans: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy. This means a greater proportion of the colliding particles have enough energy to react, so the frequency of successful collisions increases and the rate of reaction increases. The catalyst is not used up.
worked.q: Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction. (4 marks)
steps: Start with the pathway: the catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway (1).
Say what changes: this pathway has a lower activation energy (1).
Link to particles: so more particles have at least the activation energy at the same temperature (1).
Link to rate: so the frequency of successful collisions increases and the rate of reaction increases (1).

worked.ans: The activation energy falls by 50 kJ/mol; the overall energy change is still −90 kJ/mol (exothermic).
worked.q: On a reaction profile, the activation energy of an uncatalysed exothermic reaction is 120 kJ/mol. With a catalyst it is 70 kJ/mol. The overall energy change is −90 kJ/mol. Find the reduction in activation energy and the overall energy change with the catalyst. (3 marks)
steps: A catalyst does not change the energy of reactants or products (1 mark).
So the overall energy change is unchanged at −90 kJ/mol (1 mark).
